chapter_title: Maths Formula Revision (SSC / Banking / DSSSB / State PSC / Competitive Exams)

notes_list.title: Laws of indices
notes_list.trick: Convert every number to the same base first (4=2², 8=2³, 9=3², 27=3³), then just add or subtract powers.

example.question: Simplify 2^5 × 2^3 ÷ 2^6.

notes_list.title: Number of divisors
notes_list.basic_overview: If $$N=p^a q^b r^c$$, then total positive divisors $$=(a+1)(b+1)(c+1)$$.
notes_list.trick: Only perfect squares have an ODD number of divisors. Number of odd divisors = ignore the power of 2 and apply the formula.

example.question: How many divisors does 360 have?

notes_list.title: Sum of positive divisors
notes_list.trick: Work prime by prime: each prime gives a GP sum 1 + p + p² + … + p^a. Multiply the results.

example.question: Find the sum of all divisors of 12.

notes_list.title: Remainder of a power
notes_list.basic_overview: To find the remainder of $$a^n$$ divided by d, reduce a modulo d first (a ≡ r), then find the remainder of $$r^n$$ — look for a repeating cycle.
notes_list.trick: a^n ÷ (a−1) always leaves remainder 1. a^n ÷ (a+1) leaves 1 if n is even and a (i.e. −1 ≡ d−1) if n is odd.

example.question: Remainder when 7^100 is divided by 6?

notes_list.title: Unit digit of a power
notes_list.trick: Divide the power by 4 (for cyclic length 4). Remainder 1,2,3 → take 1st,2nd,3rd of the cycle; remainder 0 → take the 4th (last) of the cycle.

example.question: Unit digit of 7^123?

notes_list.title: HCF × LCM relation
notes_list.basic_overview: For exactly two positive integers a,b: $$\mathrm{HCF}(a,b)\times\mathrm{LCM}(a,b)=ab$$.
notes_list.trick: This works ONLY for two numbers, not three. HCF always divides LCM.

example.question: HCF = 12, LCM = 180, one number = 36. Find the other.

notes_list.title: Numbers from HCF and ratio
notes_list.basic_overview: If two numbers are in ratio m:n and HCF is H, numbers are $$Hm,Hn$$ provided gcd(m,n)=1. Then LCM $$=Hmn$$.
notes_list.trick: Always write numbers as Hm and Hn, then use LCM = H·m·n to link HCF, LCM and ratio.

example.question: Two numbers are in ratio 3:5 and their LCM is 150. Find the numbers.

notes_list.title: Same remainder pattern
notes_list.basic_overview: If numbers leave the same remainder r on division by d, then their pairwise differences are divisible by d. Largest such d = HCF of the differences.
notes_list.trick: Subtract the numbers, take HCF of the differences — never include the numbers themselves.

example.question: Greatest number that divides 61, 85 and 109 leaving the same remainder?

notes_list.title: Greatest divisor with given remainders
notes_list.basic_overview: Greatest number dividing a and b leaving remainders r1 and r2 = $$\mathrm{HCF}(a-r_1,\ b-r_2)$$.
notes_list.trick: Subtract each remainder from its own number first, then take the HCF.

example.question: Greatest number that divides 60 and 98 leaving remainders 4 and 2.

notes_list.title: Least number with given remainders
notes_list.basic_overview: Same remainder r in every case: LCM + r. Constant difference (divisor − remainder = k) in every case: LCM − k.
notes_list.trick: Check divisor − remainder for every divisor. If it is the same number k each time, answer = LCM − k.

example.question: Least number which leaves remainders 1, 3, 7 when divided by 6, 8, 12 respectively?

notes_list.title: Divisibility rules
notes_list.basic_overview: By 2: last digit even. By 3: digit sum divisible by 3. By 4: last two digits divisible by 4. By 5: last digit 0 or 5. By 6: divisible by 2 and 3. By 8: last three digits divisible by 8. By 9: digit sum divisible by 9. By 11: (sum of digits at odd places) − (sum at even places) is 0 or a multiple of 11.
notes_list.trick: For composite divisors use co-prime factors: 12 = 3×4, 24 = 3×8, 72 = 8×9. For 7, 11, 13 together test the number 1001 = 7×11×13.

example.question: Is 2926 divisible by 11?
example.solution: Digits from right: 6,2,9,2. Odd places 6+9 = 15; even places 2+2 = 4; difference 11 → divisible. (2926 = 11 × 266)

example.question: Find 37.5% of 480.

notes_list.title: Successive increase/decrease
notes_list.basic_overview: For changes x% and y%: $$\text{Net change}=x+y+\frac{xy}{100}$$; take decreases as negative.
notes_list.trick: Never add the percentages directly. Use +, − signs and add the small product term xy/100.

example.question: A price is raised by 20% and then reduced by 10%. Net change?

notes_list.title: Same increase and decrease
notes_list.basic_overview: Increase x% followed by decrease x% (or the reverse) gives net change $$-\frac{x^2}{100}\%$$ — always a loss.
notes_list.trick: Net loss % = x² ÷ 100. Example shortcut: 10% up and 10% down = 1% loss.

example.question: A value increases by 20% and then decreases by 20%. Net change?

notes_list.title: Population / depreciation
notes_list.basic_overview: $$V_n=V_0\left(1\pm\frac r{100}\right)^n$$, with + for growth and − for depreciation.
notes_list.trick: For 10% use factor 1.1 or 0.9, for 20% use 1.2 or 0.8, for 5% use 1.05 or 0.95. Square when n = 2.

example.question: A town of 20,000 grows 10% every year. Population after 2 years?

notes_list.title: Price rise and consumption cut
notes_list.basic_overview: If price rises by x%, consumption must fall by $$\frac{x}{100+x}\times100\%$$ to keep expenditure constant. Similarly, if A is x% more than B, then B is $$\frac{x}{100+x}\times100\%$$ less than A.
notes_list.trick: Use fractions: 25% rise = 1/4 → reduce by 1/5 = 20%. 20% rise → reduce 1/6 = 16.67%. 50% rise → reduce 1/3 = 33.33%.

example.question: Price of sugar rises by 25%. By how much should a family cut its use to keep spending the same?

notes_list.title: x% of y = y% of x
notes_list.trick: Swap to the easier one before calculating.

example.question: Find 8% of 50.

notes_list.title: Election / votes problems
notes_list.basic_overview: Winner % + loser % = 100% (if no invalid votes). Margin = (winner % − loser %) of valid votes.
notes_list.trick: Convert the margin into a percentage difference, then divide to get the total.

example.question: The winner got 55% of the votes and won by 3000 votes. Total votes?

notes_list.title: CP, SP and MP relation
notes_list.trick: Profit/loss % is always on CP; discount % is always on marked price (MP).

example.question: CP = ₹800 and profit = 25%. Find SP.

notes_list.title: Successive discounts
notes_list.basic_overview: Equivalent discount for x% and y%: $$x+y-\frac{xy}{100}\%$$.
notes_list.trick: Multiply the remaining fractions: 20% and 10% discount → 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72, so total discount 28%.

example.question: Find the single discount equal to successive discounts of 20% and 10%.

notes_list.title: CP of x articles = SP of y articles
notes_list.basic_overview: If CP of x articles equals SP of y articles, profit/loss percentage $$=\frac{x-y}{y}\times100\%$$; positive = profit, negative = loss.
notes_list.trick: Divide by the SP side (y) in the denominator.

example.question: CP of 15 articles = SP of 12 articles. Find the gain %.

notes_list.title: False weight
notes_list.basic_overview: If T units are charged while F units are actually supplied, gain % due to false weight $$=\frac{T-F}{F}\times100$$.
notes_list.trick: Error ÷ (true value − error) × 100. Denominator is the weight actually given.

example.question: A shopkeeper gives 900 g but charges for 1 kg. Gain %?

notes_list.title: Markup and discount
notes_list.basic_overview: If MP is m% above CP and discount is d%, $$\frac{SP}{CP}=\left(1+\frac m{100}\right)\left(1-\frac d{100}\right)$$.
notes_list.trick: Assume CP = 100 and apply markup then discount in order.

example.question: An article is marked 40% above cost and sold at a 20% discount. Find profit %.

notes_list.title: Dishonest dealer (profit + false weight)
notes_list.basic_overview: If a dealer charges p% profit and also uses false weight, overall gain % $$=\left(\frac{(100+p)\times\text{True weight}}{\text{False weight}}-100\right)\%$$.
notes_list.trick: Both effects multiply — never simply add the two percentages.

example.question: A dealer sells at 10% profit but uses a 900 g weight instead of 1 kg. Overall gain %?

notes_list.title: Same SP, equal profit % and loss %
notes_list.basic_overview: If two articles are sold at the same SP, one at x% profit and the other at x% loss, there is always an overall loss of $$\frac{x^2}{100}\%$$.
notes_list.trick: Same formula as 'same increase and decrease' in percentage.

example.question: Two items sold at the same price, one at 10% gain and the other at 10% loss. Overall result?

notes_list.title: Profit equals loss at two selling prices
notes_list.basic_overview: If profit at SP1 equals loss at SP2, then $$CP=\frac{SP_1+SP_2}{2}$$.
notes_list.trick: CP lies exactly in the middle of the two selling prices.

example.question: Selling at ₹400 gives the same profit as the loss when selling at ₹300. Find CP.

notes_list.title: Simple Interest
notes_list.trick: Write rate as R% per year, time in years. For months use T = months/12.

example.question: Find SI on ₹5000 at 8% for 3 years.

notes_list.title: Equal installments under SI
notes_list.basic_overview: For equal annual installments x paid at the end of each year, present value $$P=\frac{x}{1+\frac{R}{100}}+\frac{x}{1+\frac{2R}{100}}+\cdots$$
notes_list.trick: Each installment is discounted back by its time: the later it is paid, the more interest it would have earned.

example.question: Two equal installments of ₹660 are paid at the end of year 1 and year 2 at 10% SI. Find the loan.

notes_list.title: SI time-rate relation
notes_list.trick: Use ratios instead of recomputing: new SI = old SI × (R₂T₂)/(R₁T₁).

example.question: SI is ₹360 at 6% for 2 years. Find SI at 8% for 3 years on the same sum.

notes_list.title: Sum becomes n times at SI
notes_list.basic_overview: If a sum becomes n times in T years at SI, $$R=\frac{(n-1)\times100}{T}\%$$.
notes_list.trick: Sum doubles in T years → rate = 100/T. If a sum becomes k times in the same period, time scales by (k−1).

example.question: A sum doubles in 8 years at SI. Find the rate.

notes_list.title: Time to become k times at SI
notes_list.basic_overview: If a sum doubles in T years, it becomes 3 times in 2T years, 4 times in 3T years — i.e. (k−1)T years for k times.
notes_list.trick: Interest earned = (k − 1) × P, so time ∝ (k − 1).

example.question: A sum doubles in 5 years at SI. In how many years will it become 3 times?

notes_list.title: Compound amount
notes_list.trick: For R = 10%, multiply by 11/10 each year; for 20%, by 6/5; for 5%, by 21/20 — keep P as a multiple of the denominators.

example.question: Find CI on ₹10,000 at 10% for 2 years.

notes_list.title: Half-yearly compounding
notes_list.basic_overview: Use rate $$R/2$$ and number of periods $$2n$$.
notes_list.trick: Halve the rate, double the time.

example.question: Amount on ₹8000 at 10% p.a. for 1 year, compounded half-yearly?

notes_list.title: Quarterly compounding
notes_list.basic_overview: Use rate $$R/4$$ and number of periods $$4n$$.
notes_list.trick: Quarter the rate, quadruple the time.

example.question: Amount on ₹10,000 at 20% p.a. for 6 months, compounded quarterly?

notes_list.title: CI − SI for 2 years
notes_list.trick: If the difference is given, find P directly: P = difference × (100/R)².

example.question: Find CI − SI on ₹5000 at 10% for 2 years.

notes_list.title: CI − SI for 3 years
notes_list.trick: It is the 2-year difference multiplied by (3 + R/100).

example.question: Find CI − SI on ₹1000 at 10% for 3 years.

notes_list.title: Growth factor method
notes_list.basic_overview: For successive annual rates r1,r2,... multiply the factors $$\left(1+\frac{r_i}{100}\right)$$ rather than adding rates.
notes_list.trick: Convert each % into a factor, multiply, then subtract 1 to get the net growth.

example.question: A sum grows 10% in year 1 and 20% in year 2. Total growth?

notes_list.title: Composition from ratio
notes_list.basic_overview: If a:b=m:n, then $$a=\frac m{m+n}(a+b),\quad b=\frac n{m+n}(a+b)$$.
notes_list.trick: Total number of parts = m + n; one part = total ÷ (m+n).

example.question: Two numbers are in ratio 3:5 and their sum is 160. Find them.

notes_list.title: Third proportional
notes_list.trick: a : b = b : c, so the middle term is squared.

example.question: Third proportional to 4 and 6?

notes_list.title: Fourth proportional
notes_list.trick: Cross multiply: ax = bc.

example.question: Fourth proportional to 3, 4, 9?

notes_list.title: Mean proportional
notes_list.basic_overview: Mean proportional between a and b is $$\sqrt{ab}$$.
notes_list.trick: Middle term of a GP of three terms.

example.question: Mean proportional between 4 and 16?

notes_list.title: Combining ratios
notes_list.basic_overview: If a:b = p:q and b:c = r:s, make b equal: $$a:b:c=pr:qr:qs$$.
notes_list.trick: Multiply the first ratio by r and the second by q so that the common term b becomes qr.

example.question: A:B = 2:3 and B:C = 4:5. Find A:B:C.

notes_list.title: Profit-sharing ratio
notes_list.basic_overview: Profit is divided in the ratio of $$\text{Capital}\times\text{Time}$$.
notes_list.trick: If the time is equal, the ratio is the ratio of capitals; if capitals are equal, the ratio of times.

example.question: A invests ₹3000 for 12 months and B ₹4000 for 6 months. Divide a profit of ₹5000.

notes_list.title: Changing investment
notes_list.basic_overview: If A invests I1 for T1 and B invests I2 for T2, profit ratio $$=I_1T_1:I_2T_2$$.
notes_list.trick: Convert every period into months and multiply by the capital.

example.question: A starts with ₹5000. B joins after 4 months with ₹6000. Profit ratio at year-end?

notes_list.title: Alligation
notes_list.basic_overview: For cheaper C, dearer D and mean M: $$C:D=(D-M):(M-C)$$.
notes_list.trick: Draw the cross: cheaper and dearer on top, mean in the middle, subtract diagonally — the results give the ratio of cheaper : dearer.

example.question: Rice at ₹20/kg and ₹30/kg is mixed to get ₹24/kg. Find the ratio.

notes_list.title: Repeated replacement
notes_list.basic_overview: If x quantity is removed from total V and replaced n times, original substance remaining $$=V\left(1-\frac{x}{V}\right)^n$$.
notes_list.trick: Fraction left after each replacement = (V − x)/V; raise to power n.

example.question: 40 L of milk: 4 L is removed and replaced by water, done twice. Milk left?

notes_list.title: Average
notes_list.trick: Sum = Average × Number. Most average problems are solved by working with sums.

notes_list.title: Average of first n natural numbers
notes_list.trick: Average of any AP = (first + last)/2.

example.question: Average of the first 20 natural numbers?

notes_list.title: Average of first n odd numbers
notes_list.trick: Sum of first n odd numbers = n².

example.question: Average of the first 15 odd numbers?

notes_list.title: Average of first n even numbers
notes_list.trick: Sum of first n even numbers = n(n+1).

example.question: Average of the first 12 even numbers?

notes_list.title: Replacement rule
notes_list.basic_overview: If one value is replaced among n observations and average changes by d: $$\text{New value}=\text{Old value}+nd$$.
notes_list.trick: Change in total = n × change in average. Use + if average rises, − if it falls.

example.question: Average weight of 8 persons rises by 2 kg when a 60 kg person is replaced. Weight of the new person?

notes_list.title: Weighted average
notes_list.trick: Weights are the group sizes. Use alligation when only two groups are mixed.

example.question: 30 students average 60 and 20 students average 70. Combined average?

notes_list.title: Adding a new member
notes_list.basic_overview: If the average of n items changes by d when one more item is added: $$\text{New item}=\text{Old average}+(n+1)d$$.
notes_list.trick: Opposite of replacement rule: use (n+1) as the multiplier.

example.question: Average of 5 numbers is 20. A sixth number raises the average to 22. Find it.

notes_list.title: Speed-Distance-Time
notes_list.trick: Keep units consistent — convert km/h to m/s or minutes to hours before calculating.

example.question: Time to cover 150 km at 50 km/h?

notes_list.title: Unit conversion
notes_list.trick: km/h → m/s: multiply by 5/18. m/s → km/h: multiply by 18/5.

example.question: Convert 72 km/h to m/s.

notes_list.title: Average speed — equal distances
notes_list.trick: Average speed is NOT the simple mean when distances are equal; it is the harmonic mean.

example.question: A person goes at 40 km/h and returns at 60 km/h. Average speed?

notes_list.title: Average speed — equal times
notes_list.basic_overview: If equal time is spent at speeds s1 and s2, $$S_{avg}=\frac{s_1+s_2}{2}$$.
notes_list.trick: Equal time → arithmetic mean. Equal distance → harmonic mean.

example.question: A car drives 2 h at 40 km/h and 2 h at 60 km/h. Average speed?

notes_list.title: Relative speed
notes_list.trick: Overtaking → subtract; meeting/crossing head-on → add.

example.question: Two cars move at 60 and 40 km/h. Relative speed in the same direction and in opposite directions?

notes_list.title: Speed ratio and time ratio
notes_list.basic_overview: For the same distance, speed is inversely proportional to time: $$S_1:S_2=T_2:T_1$$.
notes_list.trick: Invert the speed ratio to get the time ratio, then use the given difference to find one 'part'.

example.question: Speeds of A and B are in ratio 4:5. A takes 30 minutes more. Find B's time.
example.solution: Times 5:4 → 1 part = 30 min → B takes 4 × 30 = 120 min.

notes_list.title: Meeting problems
notes_list.basic_overview: Two people start from opposite ends toward each other: $$T=\frac{D}{s_1+s_2}$$.
notes_list.trick: Distance covered together = D, so use the relative (sum) speed.

example.question: Two towns are 300 km apart. Trains start towards each other at 60 and 40 km/h. When do they meet?

notes_list.title: Circular track
notes_list.basic_overview: Same direction: first meeting after $$\frac{L}{|s_1-s_2|}$$. Opposite direction: $$\frac{L}{s_1+s_2}$$, where L is the track length.
notes_list.trick: The faster runner gains one full lap (L) over the slower one.

example.question: Two runners at 5 m/s and 3 m/s start together on a 400 m track in the same direction. When do they first meet?

notes_list.title: Train crossing pole/person
notes_list.trick: Distance = length of the train. Convert km/h to m/s first.

example.question: A 120 m train at 54 km/h crosses a pole. Time?

notes_list.title: Train crossing platform
notes_list.trick: Same rule for bridge or tunnel: add the lengths.

example.question: A 150 m train at 72 km/h crosses a 250 m platform. Time?

notes_list.title: Two trains
notes_list.trick: Add lengths; relative speed is sum (opposite) or difference (same direction).

example.question: Trains of 100 m and 150 m run in opposite directions at 54 and 36 km/h. Time to cross?

notes_list.title: Train and moving person
notes_list.basic_overview: Train and a person moving: relative speed $$=|S_{train}\pm S_{person}|$$, time $$=\frac{L}{\text{relative speed}}$$.
notes_list.trick: Person walking the same way → subtract speeds; opposite way → add.

example.question: A 150 m train at 60 km/h passes a man walking at 6 km/h in the same direction. Time?

notes_list.title: Upstream / downstream
notes_list.basic_overview: With boat speed u and stream speed v: $$D=u+v,\qquad U=u-v$$
notes_list.trick: Downstream helps (add); upstream opposes (subtract).

example.question: Boat speed 10 km/h, stream 2 km/h. Downstream and upstream speeds?

notes_list.title: Boat and stream speeds
notes_list.trick: Boat = average of the two speeds; stream = half the difference.

example.question: Downstream 15 km/h, upstream 9 km/h. Find boat and stream speeds.

notes_list.title: Round trip time
notes_list.basic_overview: Time for a round trip of distance D each way: $$T=\frac{D}{u+v}+\frac{D}{u-v}$$.
notes_list.trick: Compute both legs separately; don't use average speed directly.

example.question: Boat speed 8 km/h, stream 2 km/h, distance 30 km each way. Total time?

notes_list.title: One-day work
notes_list.basic_overview: If A completes work in n days, one-day work $$=1/n$$.
notes_list.trick: Always think in 'work per day'; total work = 1.

example.question: A completes a job in 10 days. How much does he do in 1 day?

notes_list.title: Combined work
notes_list.basic_overview: If A and B take a and b days: $$T=\frac{ab}{a+b}$$.
notes_list.trick: For three workers use 1/T = 1/a + 1/b + 1/c.

example.question: A takes 12 days and B takes 6 days. Together?

notes_list.title: LCM (unit) method
notes_list.basic_overview: Take total work = LCM of the days. Daily work = Total ÷ days.
notes_list.trick: This avoids fractions completely and is the fastest method in exams.

example.question: A takes 20 days, B takes 30 days. Together?

notes_list.title: Efficiency relation
notes_list.basic_overview: Efficiency is inversely proportional to time: $$E_1:E_2=T_2:T_1$$.
notes_list.trick: If A is twice as efficient as B, A takes half the time of B.

example.question: A is twice as efficient as B. Together they finish in 12 days. A alone?
example.solution: Efficiency 2:1 = 3 units/day × 12 = 36 units; A alone = 36/2 = 18 days.

notes_list.title: Men-days-hours
notes_list.trick: Man-days (or man-hours) is the constant amount of work.

example.question: 12 men finish a job in 15 days. How many men are needed to finish it in 10 days?

notes_list.title: Wages
notes_list.basic_overview: Wages are divided in the ratio of work done (efficiency × days).
notes_list.trick: Find the efficiency ratio via the LCM method, then split the money in that ratio.

example.question: A can finish a job in 10 days and B in 15 days. They share ₹1500. Find each share.
example.solution: Efficiency ratio 3:2 (when working equal days) → A ₹900, B ₹600.

notes_list.title: Leaving the work midway
notes_list.basic_overview: Add the work done by each person for the days they worked; set the total equal to 1 (or the LCM units).
notes_list.trick: Let total time be x days and write each person's days in terms of x.

example.question: A takes 20 days, B takes 30 days. They start together, but A leaves 5 days before completion. Total time?

notes_list.title: Filling pipe
notes_list.basic_overview: If a pipe fills in a hours, rate $$=1/a$$ tank per hour.
notes_list.trick: Same as one-day work — filling is +, emptying is −.

example.question: A pipe fills a tank in 6 hours. Part filled in 1 hour?

notes_list.title: Filling + emptying
notes_list.basic_overview: If fill time is a and empty time is b (b>a), net time $$=\frac{ab}{b-a}$$.
notes_list.trick: If emptying is faster than filling, the tank never fills.

example.question: A pipe fills in 12 h and an outlet empties in 18 h. Both open — time to fill?

notes_list.title: Multiple pipes
notes_list.basic_overview: Net rate = sum of filling rates − sum of emptying rates.
notes_list.trick: Use the LCM method with units per hour.

example.question: Pipes A and B fill in 10 h and 15 h; pipe C empties in 30 h. All open — time to fill?
example.solution: LCM 30 units: A=3, B=2, C=−1 → net 4/h → 30/4 = 7.5 hours.

notes_list.title: Leak problems
notes_list.basic_overview: If a tank fills in a hours normally but takes b hours with a leak, the leak alone empties it in $$\frac{ab}{b-a}$$ hours.
notes_list.trick: Leak rate = normal rate − actual rate.

example.question: A tank fills in 6 h, but with a leak it takes 8 h. How long does the leak take to empty a full tank?

notes_list.title: Squares
notes_list.trick: a² + b² = (a+b)² − 2ab = (a−b)² + 2ab.

example.question: If a + b = 10 and ab = 21, find a² + b².

notes_list.title: Difference of squares
notes_list.trick: Use for fast squares and products: 101² − 99² = 200 × 2.

example.question: Evaluate 101² − 99².

notes_list.title: Cubes
notes_list.trick: When a+b and ab are given, use the (a+b)³ form directly.

example.question: If a + b = 5 and ab = 6, find a³ + b³.

notes_list.title: Three-variable identity
notes_list.trick: Whenever a+b+c = 0, directly write the cube sum = 3abc.

example.question: If a = 2, b = 3, c = −5, find a³ + b³ + c³.

notes_list.title: Square identity
notes_list.trick: Square the given expression and subtract 2.

example.question: If x + 1/x = 3, find x² + 1/x².

notes_list.title: Cube identity
notes_list.trick: Memorise n³ − 3n directly.

example.question: If x + 1/x = 3, find x³ + 1/x³.

notes_list.title: Minus form
notes_list.trick: Minus form → add 2 instead of subtracting.

example.question: If x − 1/x = 4, find x² + 1/x².

notes_list.title: Reverse: from x² + 1/x² to x + 1/x
notes_list.trick: Use +2 for the sum form and −2 for the difference form.

example.question: If x² + 1/x² = 14, find x + 1/x.

notes_list.title: Quadratic formula
notes_list.trick: First try splitting the middle term; use the formula only if factoring fails.

example.question: Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0.

notes_list.title: Nature of roots
notes_list.basic_overview: Discriminant $$D=b^2-4ac$$: D>0 distinct real roots; D=0 equal real roots; D<0 non-real roots.
notes_list.trick: D is a perfect square → roots are rational.

example.question: Nature of roots of x² + 4x + 5 = 0?

notes_list.title: Sum and product of roots
notes_list.trick: Sum = −(coefficient of x)/(coefficient of x²); product = constant/(coefficient of x²).

example.question: Find the sum and product of the roots of x² − 7x + 10 = 0.

notes_list.title: Forming a quadratic from roots
notes_list.trick: Always write 'x² − (sum)x + product'.

example.question: Form the quadratic whose roots are 3 and 4.

notes_list.title: Expressions in roots
notes_list.trick: Never solve for the roots — use sum and product only.

example.question: For x² − 5x + 6 = 0 find α² + β².

notes_list.title: Product and quotient
notes_list.basic_overview: $$\sqrt a\sqrt b=\sqrt{ab},\qquad\frac{\sqrt a}{\sqrt b}=\sqrt{\frac ab}$$ for b>0.
notes_list.trick: Multiply or divide under one root, then simplify to a perfect square.

example.question: Simplify √18 × √2.

notes_list.title: Rationalisation
notes_list.basic_overview: $$\frac1{\sqrt a}=\frac{\sqrt a}{a}$$ and use the conjugate for binomial surds.
notes_list.trick: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate; (√a − √b)(√a + √b) = a − b.

example.question: Rationalise 1/(√3 − 1).

notes_list.title: Nested surd
notes_list.trick: Find two numbers with sum a and product b.

example.question: Simplify √(7 + 2√12).

notes_list.title: Comparing surds
notes_list.basic_overview: Convert surds to the same order (LCM of the roots), then compare the numbers under the root.
notes_list.trick: Raise both to the LCM of their orders: √2 and ∛3 → raise to power 6.

example.question: Which is greater: √2 or ∛3?

notes_list.title: Infinite nested root
notes_list.trick: Replace the infinite expression by n and solve the quadratic (take the positive root).

notes_list.title: Fractional powers
notes_list.trick: Take the root first, then the power — numbers stay small.

notes_list.title: Negative powers
notes_list.trick: Flip the base to remove the negative sign.

example.question: Value of 2^(−3)?

notes_list.title: Zero power
notes_list.trick: Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1.

example.question: Value of 999⁰ + 5⁰?

notes_list.title: Equal bases
notes_list.trick: Express both sides with the same base, then equate the powers.

notes_list.title: nth term of AP
notes_list.trick: Common difference d = any term − the previous term.

example.question: Find the 20th term of 5, 8, 11, …

notes_list.title: Sum of n terms
notes_list.trick: If first and last terms are known use n/2 × (a + l).

example.question: Sum of the first 20 terms of 5, 8, 11, …

notes_list.title: Arithmetic mean
notes_list.trick: Middle term = average of its neighbours.

example.question: 7, x, 19 are in AP. Find x.

notes_list.title: Number of terms in AP
notes_list.trick: Divide the gap between first and last term by d, then add 1.

example.question: How many terms in 7, 14, 21, …, 98?

notes_list.title: Count of multiples
notes_list.basic_overview: Number of multiples of k up to N $$=\left\lfloor\frac Nk\right\rfloor$$.
notes_list.trick: Divide and ignore the remainder.

example.question: How many multiples of 7 up to 200?

notes_list.title: Sum of first n natural numbers
notes_list.trick: Use for sums like 1 to 100 instantly.

notes_list.title: Sum of squares
notes_list.trick: Memorise as n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.

example.question: Find 1² + 2² + … + 10².

notes_list.title: Sum of cubes
notes_list.trick: Sum of cubes = (sum of numbers)².

example.question: Find 1³ + 2³ + … + 5³.

notes_list.title: nth term of GP
notes_list.trick: Common ratio r = any term ÷ the previous term.

example.question: Find the 6th term of 2, 6, 18, …

notes_list.title: Sum of n terms
notes_list.trick: Use (r^n − 1)/(r − 1) when r > 1 and (1 − r^n)/(1 − r) when r < 1.

example.question: Sum of first 5 terms of 3, 6, 12, …

notes_list.title: Infinite GP
notes_list.trick: Check |r| < 1 before using. Recurring decimals are infinite GPs.

example.question: Sum to infinity of 8, 4, 2, …

notes_list.title: Angle sum
notes_list.trick: Exterior angle = sum of the two opposite interior angles.

example.question: Two angles of a triangle are 50° and 60°. Find the third.

diagram.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 190' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='45,145 255,145 150,30' fill='#eff6ff' stroke='#2563eb' stroke-width='3'/><text x='150' y='22' font-size='15' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e293b'>A</text><text x='30' y='158' font-size='15' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e293b'>B</text><text x='270' y='158' font-size='15' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e293b'>C</text><text x='150' y='125' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='#dc2626'>A + B + C = 180°</text></svg>
diagram.caption: Triangle ABC: the three interior angles add up to 180°.

example.question: Legs of a right triangle are 6 and 8. Find the hypotenuse.

notes_list.title: Area of triangle
notes_list.trick: Any side can be the base — use the perpendicular height to it.

example.question: Base 10 cm, height 6 cm. Area?

notes_list.title: Heron's formula
notes_list.trick: Use when all three sides are given and there is no height.

example.question: Area of a triangle with sides 13, 14, 15.

notes_list.title: Similar triangles
notes_list.basic_overview: Corresponding sides are proportional; areas of similar triangles are proportional to the squares of corresponding sides.
notes_list.trick: Side ratio a:b → area ratio a²:b².

example.question: Sides of two similar triangles are in the ratio 2:3. Ratio of areas?

notes_list.title: Equilateral triangle
notes_list.trick: Each angle is 60°; the altitude also bisects the base.

example.question: Area of an equilateral triangle of side 4 cm?

notes_list.title: Exterior angle property
notes_list.basic_overview: Exterior angle of a triangle = sum of the two opposite interior angles.
notes_list.trick: Saves finding the third angle.

example.question: Two interior opposite angles are 40° and 60°. Exterior angle?

notes_list.title: Triangle centres and angles
notes_list.basic_overview: Incentre I: $$\angle BIC=90^\circ+\frac A2$$. Circumcentre O: $$\angle BOC=2A$$. Orthocentre H: $$\angle BHC=180^\circ-A$$.
notes_list.trick: Centroid divides each median 2:1 from the vertex.

example.question: In triangle ABC, ∠A = 60°. Find ∠BIC where I is the incentre.

notes_list.title: Right triangle radii
notes_list.trick: Circumcentre of a right triangle is the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

example.question: Find r and R for a right triangle with sides 6, 8, 10.

notes_list.title: Angle bisector theorem
notes_list.trick: The bisector divides the opposite side in the ratio of the other two sides.

example.question: AB = 6, AC = 9, BC = 10. AD bisects ∠A. Find BD.

notes_list.title: Basic proportionality (Thales) theorem
notes_list.trick: A line parallel to one side divides the other two sides proportionally.

example.question: DE ∥ BC, AD = 3, DB = 6, AE = 2. Find EC.

notes_list.title: Sum of interior angles
notes_list.trick: Split the polygon into (n − 2) triangles.

example.question: Sum of interior angles of a hexagon?

notes_list.title: Each interior angle of regular polygon
notes_list.trick: Interior angle = 180° − exterior angle.

example.question: Each interior angle of a regular octagon?

notes_list.title: Exterior angle of regular polygon
notes_list.trick: If the exterior angle is given, n = 360 ÷ exterior angle.

example.question: Exterior angle is 36°. Number of sides?

notes_list.title: Quadrilateral angle sum
notes_list.trick: A quadrilateral = 2 triangles.

example.question: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 80°, 90°, 100°. Find the fourth.

notes_list.title: Number of diagonals
notes_list.trick: Each vertex joins to (n − 3) others; divide by 2 because each diagonal is counted twice.

example.question: Diagonals in an octagon?

notes_list.title: Radius and tangent
notes_list.basic_overview: Radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent. Tangent length from an external point at distance d: $$\sqrt{d^2-r^2}$$.
notes_list.trick: Tangents from the same external point are equal.

example.question: A point is 13 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. Length of the tangent?

notes_list.title: Angle in semicircle
notes_list.basic_overview: Angle subtended by a diameter at the circumference is $$90^\circ$$.
notes_list.trick: Diameter seen at any point on the circle → right angle.

example.question: AB is a diameter and C is a point on the circle. Find ∠ACB.

notes_list.title: Chord and center
notes_list.basic_overview: Perpendicular from center to a chord bisects the chord.
notes_list.trick: Join the centre to the chord's end to form a right triangle.

example.question: A 16 cm chord is 6 cm from the centre. Find the radius.

notes_list.title: Angle at centre
notes_list.basic_overview: Angle at the centre = 2 × angle at the circumference on the same arc.
notes_list.trick: Angles in the same segment are equal.

example.question: An angle at the circumference is 40°. Angle at the centre on the same arc?

notes_list.title: Cyclic quadrilateral
notes_list.basic_overview: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to $$180^\circ$$; exterior angle = interior opposite angle.
notes_list.trick: Opposite angles are supplementary.

example.question: In cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, ∠A = 70°. Find ∠C.

notes_list.title: Common tangents
notes_list.basic_overview: For two circles with centres d apart and radii R, r: direct common tangent $$\sqrt{d^2-(R-r)^2}$$, transverse common tangent $$\sqrt{d^2-(R+r)^2}$$.
notes_list.trick: Direct → subtract radii; transverse → add radii.

example.question: d = 13, R = 7, r = 2. Length of the direct common tangent?

notes_list.title: Basic ratios
notes_list.trick: Remember 'PHB' – Pandit Har Prasad Badri Prasad Har Har Bole: sin=P/H, cos=B/H, tan=P/B.

example.question: Right triangle with P = 3, B = 4, H = 5. Find sin θ and tan θ.

notes_list.title: Reciprocal ratios
notes_list.trick: Pairs: sin↔cosec, cos↔sec, tan↔cot.

example.question: If cos θ = 4/5, find sec θ.

notes_list.title: Pythagorean identities
notes_list.trick: Also (sec θ − tan θ)(sec θ + tan θ) = 1.

example.question: If tan θ = 3/4, find sec θ.

notes_list.title: Double angle
notes_list.trick: Use sin 2θ = 2 tan θ/(1 + tan²θ) when only tan θ is given.

example.question: Verify sin 60° using sin 30° and cos 30°.

notes_list.title: Standard values
notes_list.trick: sin values = √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2. For cos reverse the order.

example.question: Evaluate sin 30° cos 60° + cos 30° sin 60°.

notes_list.title: Complementary angles
notes_list.trick: If two angles add up to 90°, sin(one)/cos(other) = 1 and tan × cot = 1.

example.question: Find the value of sin 35° / cos 55°.

notes_list.title: Angle of elevation
notes_list.trick: Draw the right triangle first; angle of elevation = angle of depression from the top (alternate angles).

example.question: From a point 30 m from the foot of a tower the angle of elevation is 45°. Height?

notes_list.title: Two observation points
notes_list.basic_overview: If angles α and β (α < β) are seen at two points d apart (on the same side): $$h=\frac{d}{\cot\alpha-\cot\beta}$$.
notes_list.trick: Write h = x tan β and h = (x + d) tan α, then subtract.

example.question: A tower is seen at 30°; after moving 20 m closer it is seen at 60°. Find the height.

notes_list.title: Square
notes_list.trick: If the diagonal is d, area = d²/2.

example.question: Side = 7 cm. Area and diagonal?

notes_list.title: Rectangle
notes_list.trick: For a fixed perimeter, a square gives the maximum area.

example.question: l = 12, b = 5. Area and diagonal?

notes_list.title: Triangle
notes_list.basic_overview: Area $$=\frac12bh$$; Heron's formula may be used when all three sides are known.
notes_list.trick: Isosceles triangle: drop the altitude on the base to get a right triangle.

example.question: Triangle with sides 5, 5, 6. Area?

notes_list.title: Circle
notes_list.trick: Use π = 22/7 when the radius is a multiple of 7.

example.question: r = 7 cm. Area and circumference?

notes_list.title: Semicircle
notes_list.basic_overview: Area $$=\frac12\pi r^2$$; curved length $$=\pi r$$; full perimeter $$=(\pi+2)r$$.
notes_list.trick: Don't forget to add the diameter 2r for the full perimeter.

example.question: Area and perimeter of a semicircle with r = 7 cm.

notes_list.title: Trapezium
notes_list.trick: Average of the parallel sides × height.

example.question: Parallel sides 10 and 14 cm, height 8 cm. Area?

notes_list.title: Rhombus
notes_list.trick: Diagonals bisect each other at right angles.

example.question: Diagonals 10 and 24 cm. Area and side?

notes_list.title: Sector of a circle
notes_list.trick: Take the fraction θ/360 of the full circle.

example.question: Sector angle 90°, r = 14 cm. Area and arc length?

notes_list.title: Parallelogram
notes_list.trick: Use the perpendicular height, not the slant side.

example.question: Base 12 cm, height 5 cm. Area?

notes_list.title: Regular hexagon
notes_list.trick: A regular hexagon is made of 6 equilateral triangles.

example.question: Area of a regular hexagon with side 2 cm?

notes_list.title: Cube
notes_list.trick: If side is doubled, volume becomes 8 times and surface area 4 times.

example.question: Cube of side 5 cm: volume, TSA and diagonal?

notes_list.title: Cuboid
notes_list.trick: LSA = 2h(l + b).

example.question: Cuboid 12 × 4 × 3: volume, TSA and diagonal?

notes_list.title: Cylinder
notes_list.basic_overview: Volume $$=\pi r^2h$$, CSA $$=2\pi rh$$, TSA $$=2\pi r(r+h)$$.
notes_list.trick: CSA is a rectangle of size 2πr × h when unrolled.

example.question: r = 7 cm, h = 10 cm: volume and CSA?

diagram.caption: Cylinder radius r and height h.

notes_list.title: Cone
notes_list.basic_overview: Volume $$=\frac13\pi r^2h$$, CSA $$=\pi rl$$, TSA $$=\pi r(r+l)$$, $$l=\sqrt{r^2+h^2}$$.
notes_list.trick: Cone volume = 1/3 of the cylinder with the same r and h.

example.question: Cone with r = 3 cm, h = 4 cm: slant height, volume and CSA?
example.solution: l = 5 cm; V = ⅓π × 9 × 4 = 12π cm³; CSA = π × 3 × 5 = 15π cm².

notes_list.title: Sphere
notes_list.trick: Surface area of a sphere = 4 × area of its great circle.

example.question: Surface area of a sphere of radius 21 cm?

notes_list.title: Hemisphere
notes_list.basic_overview: Volume $$=\frac23\pi r^3$$, CSA $$=2\pi r^2$$, TSA $$=3\pi r^2$$.
notes_list.trick: TSA = CSA + the circular base πr².

example.question: r = 7 cm: CSA and TSA of a hemisphere?

notes_list.title: Frustum
notes_list.trick: Frustum = big cone − small cone.

example.question: Frustum with R = 4, r = 1, h = 4. Find the volume.

notes_list.title: Unit conversion in area
notes_list.basic_overview: If length unit changes by factor k, area changes by $$k^2$$. 1 m² = 10,000 cm².
notes_list.trick: Square the length conversion factor.

example.question: Convert 2.5 m² to cm².

notes_list.title: Unit conversion in volume
notes_list.basic_overview: If length unit changes by factor k, volume changes by $$k^3$$. 1 m³ = 1000 litres = 10⁶ cm³.
notes_list.trick: 1 litre = 1000 cm³.

example.question: A tank is 2 m × 1 m × 1 m. Capacity in litres?

notes_list.title: Path / border problems
notes_list.basic_overview: For an outer and inner rectangle/circle, area of path = outer area − inner area.
notes_list.trick: Outside path adds 2w to each dimension; inside path subtracts 2w.

example.question: A 20 m × 15 m garden has a 2 m wide path outside. Area of the path?

notes_list.title: Melting and recasting
notes_list.basic_overview: When a solid is melted and recast, volume remains constant: $$V_{old}=V_{new}$$.
notes_list.trick: Number of small solids = big volume ÷ small volume.

example.question: A sphere of radius 6 cm is melted into small spheres of radius 2 cm. How many?

notes_list.title: Classical probability
notes_list.basic_overview: For equally likely outcomes, $$P(E)=\frac{\text{favourable outcomes}}{\text{total outcomes}}$$
notes_list.trick: List the sample space first, then count favourable outcomes carefully.

example.question: A die is thrown. Probability of getting a prime number?

notes_list.title: Complement
notes_list.trick: For 'at least one' type questions, find the complement first.

example.question: Probability of rain is 0.3. Probability of no rain?

notes_list.title: Impossible and certain events
notes_list.trick: Probability can never be negative or greater than 1.

example.question: Probability of getting 7 on a single die throw?

notes_list.title: Two dice — sum table
notes_list.basic_overview: Total outcomes 36. Number of ways for sum 2,3,4,...,12 = 1,2,3,4,5,6,5,4,3,2,1.
notes_list.trick: Sum 7 has the most ways (6).

example.question: Two dice are thrown. Probability that the sum is 7?

notes_list.title: Playing-card facts
notes_list.basic_overview: 52 cards: 4 suits of 13 (26 red, 26 black); 12 face cards (J, Q, K); 4 aces; 4 kings.
notes_list.trick: Memorise: 13 per suit, 12 face cards.

example.question: Probability of drawing a face card?

notes_list.title: Odds
notes_list.trick: Odds are favourable : unfavourable — not favourable : total.

example.question: Odds in favour of an event are 3:5. Find the probability.

notes_list.title: Addition theorem
notes_list.trick: OR → add (subtract the overlap).

notes_list.title: Mutually exclusive events
notes_list.basic_overview: If A and B cannot occur together, $$P(A\cap B)=0$$ and $$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)$$.
notes_list.trick: Same card can't be both a heart and a spade.

example.question: Probability of drawing a heart or a spade?

notes_list.title: Multiplication theorem
notes_list.trick: AND → multiply. For draws without replacement, reduce both the favourable and total counts.

example.question: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue balls. Two are drawn without replacement. Probability both are red?

notes_list.title: Independent events
notes_list.basic_overview: If A and B are independent, $$P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$$.
notes_list.trick: Events like separate coin tosses or dice throws are independent.

example.question: A coin and a die are tossed. P(head and a 6)?

notes_list.title: Conditional probability
notes_list.trick: The sample space shrinks to B.

example.question: P(A∩B) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.6. Find P(A|B).

notes_list.title: Bayes theorem
notes_list.trick: Draw a tree: multiply along each path, then take the path of interest ÷ all paths that lead to B.

example.question: Machine A makes 60% of items (2% defective), B makes 40% (5% defective). An item is defective — P(it came from A)?

notes_list.title: At least one occurrence
notes_list.basic_overview: For n independent trials with event probability p, $$P(\text{at least one})=1-(1-p)^n$$.
notes_list.trick: At least one = 1 − P(none).

example.question: A coin is tossed 3 times. P(at least one head)?

notes_list.title: Exactly r successes
notes_list.basic_overview: For n independent trials with success probability p: $$P(X=r)={}^{n}C_{r}\,p^r(1-p)^{n-r}$$.
notes_list.trick: Choose which r trials succeed, then multiply by their probabilities.

example.question: A coin is tossed 3 times. P(exactly 2 heads)?

notes_list.title: At least r successes
notes_list.trick: Use the complement if it has fewer terms.

example.question: A coin is tossed 3 times. P(at least 2 heads)?

notes_list.title: Expected value of binomial
notes_list.trick: Mean = np; variance = npq.

example.question: A coin is tossed 10 times. Find E(X) and Var(X) for the number of heads.
Find 5!.

notes_list.title: Useful factorial ratio
notes_list.trick: Cancel the common tail instead of expanding both factorials.

example.question: Evaluate 10!/8!.

notes_list.title: Fundamental principle of counting
notes_list.basic_overview: If one task can be done in m ways and another in n ways: AND → m × n; OR → m + n.
notes_list.trick: AND means multiply, OR means add.

example.question: 3 shirts and 4 trousers: how many outfits?

notes_list.title: Permutation of n objects taken r
notes_list.trick: Start from n and write r factors going down.

example.question: Find 5P3.

notes_list.title: All n distinct objects
notes_list.trick: Fill positions one by one: n choices, then n−1, and so on.

example.question: In how many ways can 4 distinct books be arranged on a shelf?

notes_list.title: Repeated objects
notes_list.basic_overview: If n objects contain repetitions p,q,r,..., arrangements $$=\frac{n!}{p!q!r!\cdots}$$.
notes_list.trick: Divide by the factorial of each repeated letter's count.

example.question: Arrangements of the letters of LEVEL?

notes_list.title: Circular permutation
notes_list.basic_overview: For n distinct objects around a circle, arrangements $$=(n-1)!$$. For a necklace/garland (flippable): $$\frac{(n-1)!}{2}$$.
notes_list.trick: Fix one person to remove the rotations.

example.question: In how many ways can 6 people sit at a round table?

notes_list.title: Items together
notes_list.basic_overview: Treat the items that must be together as one block, arrange all blocks, then multiply by the arrangements inside the block.
notes_list.trick: (Number of units)! × (arrangements within the block)!

example.question: Arrangements of DELHI with the vowels together?
example.solution: Units: D, L, H, [EI] = 4! = 24; vowels inside 2! = 2 → 48.

notes_list.title: Combination
notes_list.trick: Use the smaller of r and n−r to compute fast.

example.question: Find 6C2.

notes_list.title: Symmetry
notes_list.trick: 10C8 is easier as 10C2.

example.question: Find 10C8.

notes_list.title: Relation with permutation
notes_list.trick: Selection first (C), then arrangement (× r!).

example.question: Verify 5P2 using 5C2.

notes_list.title: Pascal identity
notes_list.trick: Adding two adjacent entries in Pascal's triangle gives the entry below.

example.question: Find 5C2 + 5C1.

notes_list.title: Handshakes / matches
notes_list.trick: Every pair is counted once.

example.question: 10 people shake hands with each other once. Number of handshakes?

notes_list.title: Committee with 'at least' condition
notes_list.trick: At least one woman = total − all men.

example.question: A committee of 3 is chosen from 5 men and 4 women with at least 1 woman. How many ways?

notes_list.title: Mean
notes_list.trick: Add or subtract a constant from all values → mean changes by the same constant.

notes_list.title: Weighted mean
notes_list.trick: Weights = frequencies.

example.question: Marks 10, 20, 30 with frequencies 2, 3, 5. Find the mean.

notes_list.title: Median — odd n
notes_list.basic_overview: After arranging data, median is the $$\frac{n+1}{2}$$th observation.
notes_list.trick: Always sort the data first.

example.question: Median of 3, 9, 5, 7, 1?

notes_list.title: Median — even n
notes_list.basic_overview: Median = average of $$\frac n2$$th and $$\left(\frac n2+1\right)$$th observations.
notes_list.trick: Average the two middle values.

example.question: Median of 2, 4, 6, 8?

notes_list.title: Mode empirical relation
notes_list.trick: Mean − Mode = 3 (Mean − Median).

example.question: Mean = 20, Median = 22. Find the mode.

notes_list.title: Grouped mean
notes_list.basic_overview: $$\bar x=\frac{\sum fx}{\sum f}$$, where x is the class mark (mid-value).
notes_list.trick: Class mark = (upper limit + lower limit)/2.

example.question: Classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30 with f = 2, 3, 5. Find the mean.

notes_list.title: Grouped median
notes_list.trick: Find N/2, locate the class where the cumulative frequency first exceeds it — that is the median class.

example.question: Classes 0–10 … 40–50 with f = 5, 8, 15, 8, 4 (N = 40). Find the median.

notes_list.title: Grouped mode
notes_list.trick: Modal class = class with the highest frequency.

example.question: Same data as above. Find the mode.

notes_list.title: Range
notes_list.trick: Only uses the two extreme values.

example.question: Range of 3, 9, 12, 20?

notes_list.title: Variance
notes_list.trick: Equivalent: σ² = (Σx²/n) − (mean)².

notes_list.title: Standard deviation
notes_list.trick: SD has the same unit as the data.

example.question: Variance is 4. Standard deviation?

notes_list.title: Coefficient of variation
notes_list.trick: Smaller CV → more consistent data.

example.question: Mean = 50, SD = 10. Find CV.

notes_list.title: Effect of changing all values
notes_list.basic_overview: If every value is multiplied by k and increased by c: new mean = k·mean + c, new SD = |k|·SD.
notes_list.trick: Adding a constant does not change SD or variance.

example.question: Mean 12, SD 3. Each value is doubled and then increased by 1. New mean and SD?

notes_list.title: Union
notes_list.basic_overview: $$A\cup B$$ contains elements in A or B or both.
notes_list.trick: Write each common element only once.

notes_list.title: Intersection
notes_list.basic_overview: $$A\cap B$$ contains elements common to A and B.
notes_list.trick: Only keep elements present in both sets.

diagram.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 190' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='125' cy='95' r='65' fill='#2563eb' fill-opacity='0.2' stroke='#2563eb' stroke-width='3'/><circle cx='195' cy='95' r='65' fill='#16a34a' fill-opacity='0.2' stroke='#16a34a' stroke-width='3'/><text x='92' y='100' font-size='16'>A</text><text x='214' y='100' font-size='16'>B</text><text x='160' y='100' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='#dc2626'>A∩B</text></svg>

notes_list.title: Difference
notes_list.basic_overview: $$A-B$$ contains elements in A but not in B.
notes_list.trick: A − B = A − (A∩B).

notes_list.title: Complement
notes_list.trick: n(Aᶜ) = n(U) − n(A).

notes_list.title: De Morgan's laws
notes_list.trick: Complement flips union ↔ intersection.

notes_list.title: Two-set counting
notes_list.trick: Neither = Total − n(A∪B). Only A = n(A) − n(A∩B).

example.question: In a class of 60, 35 like tea, 30 like coffee and 10 like both. How many like neither?

notes_list.title: Three-set inclusion-exclusion
notes_list.basic_overview: $$n(A\cup B\cup C)=n(A)+n(B)+n(C)-n(A\cap B)-n(B\cap C)-n(C\cap A)+n(A\cap B\cap C)$$.
notes_list.trick: Singles − pairs + triple.

example.question: n(A) = 20, n(B) = 15, n(C) = 10, pairwise overlaps 5, 4, 3, triple overlap 2. Find n(A∪B∪C).

notes_list.title: Power set
notes_list.basic_overview: A set with n elements has $$2^n$$ subsets; $$2^n-1$$ proper subsets.
notes_list.trick: Each element is either in or out — 2 choices each.

example.question: A set has 4 elements. How many subsets and proper subsets?

notes_list.title: Distance formula
notes_list.trick: It is Pythagoras on the horizontal and vertical differences.

example.question: Distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6)?

notes_list.title: Midpoint
notes_list.trick: Average the x's and average the y's separately.

example.question: Midpoint of (2, 4) and (8, 10)?

notes_list.title: Section formula — internal
notes_list.basic_overview: If P divides A(x1,y1),B(x2,y2) in m:n, $$P=\left(\frac{mx_2+nx_1}{m+n},\frac{my_2+ny_1}{m+n}\right)$$.
notes_list.trick: Cross-multiply: m goes with the second point, n with the first.

example.question: Find the point dividing (1, 2) and (7, 8) in the ratio 1:2.

notes_list.title: Slope
notes_list.basic_overview: $$m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$$ (= tan of the angle with the positive x-axis).
notes_list.trick: Slope of the x-axis is 0; the y-axis has undefined slope.

example.question: Slope through (1, 2) and (3, 8)?

notes_list.title: Centroid of a triangle
notes_list.trick: Average all three x's and all three y's.

notes_list.title: Slope-intercept form
notes_list.trick: For ax + by + c = 0, slope = −a/b.

example.question: Line with slope 2 and y-intercept 3. Find y when x = 4.

notes_list.title: Point-slope form
notes_list.trick: Use when a point and the slope are given.

example.question: Line through (1, 2) with slope 3.

notes_list.title: Parallel lines
notes_list.basic_overview: Parallel non-vertical lines have equal slopes.
notes_list.trick: Parallel line: change only the constant term.

example.question: Line parallel to y = 3x + 1 through (0, 5)?

notes_list.title: Perpendicular lines
notes_list.trick: Flip the slope and change the sign.

example.question: A line has slope 2. Slope of a perpendicular line?

notes_list.title: Distance of a point from a line
notes_list.basic_overview: Distance of (x1,y1) from ax + by + c = 0: $$\frac{|ax_1+by_1+c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$$.
notes_list.trick: Put the line in the form ax + by + c = 0 first.

example.question: Distance of the origin from 3x + 4y − 10 = 0?

notes_list.title: Intercept form
notes_list.basic_overview: $$\frac xa+\frac yb=1$$ where a and b are the x- and y-intercepts.
notes_list.trick: Area of the triangle formed with the axes = ½|ab|.

example.question: Line through (3, 0) and (0, 4)?

notes_list.title: Triangle area
notes_list.trick: Area = 0 means the three points are collinear.

example.question: Area of triangle (0,0), (4,0), (0,3)?

notes_list.title: Collinearity test
notes_list.basic_overview: Three points are collinear if the area formula gives 0 (or their slopes are equal).
notes_list.trick: Check equal slopes first — it is faster.

example.question: Are (1,1), (2,2), (3,3) collinear?

notes_list.title: BODMAS
notes_list.basic_overview: Bracket → Orders → Division → Multiplication → Addition → Subtraction.
notes_list.trick: Division and multiplication have equal priority — go left to right. Same for addition and subtraction.

example.question: Simplify 8 + 2 × (10 − 4)² ÷ 3.

notes_list.title: Fraction operations
notes_list.trick: Cancel common factors before multiplying.

notes_list.title: Division shortcuts
notes_list.basic_overview: Divide by 5: ×2 then ÷10; divide by 25: ×4 then ÷100; divide by 125: ×8 then ÷1000.
notes_list.trick: Convert divisions into multiplications by 2, 4 or 8.

notes_list.title: Square of numbers ending in 5
notes_list.basic_overview: For a number n5: square = n(n+1) followed by 25.
notes_list.trick: Multiply the leading digits by the next number, then write 25.

example.question: Find 75².

notes_list.title: Squares near 50
notes_list.basic_overview: For 50 + d: square = (25 + d) followed by d² (two digits). For 50 − d: (25 − d) followed by d².
notes_list.trick: Works for d up to about 9.

example.question: Find 52².

notes_list.title: Product around a middle number
notes_list.trick: Use for numbers symmetric around a number with an easy square.

example.question: Find 49 × 51.

notes_list.title: Multiply by 11
notes_list.basic_overview: Write the first digit, then sum of each adjacent pair, then the last digit (carry if needed).
notes_list.trick: ab × 11 = a (a+b) b.

example.question: Find 53 × 11.

notes_list.title: Multiply by 9, 99, 999
notes_list.trick: Round up to the next power of 10 and subtract once.

example.question: Find 47 × 99.

notes_list.title: Approximation
notes_list.basic_overview: Round each number to the nearest convenient value before calculating.
notes_list.trick: Round numbers close to 10, 50, 100 and compute; check options for the nearest answer.

example.question: Approximate 49.8 × 20.1.

notes_list.title: Digital root
notes_list.basic_overview: Repeatedly sum digits until one digit remains; multiples of 9 have digital root 9 (except 0).
notes_list.trick: Use it to check multiplication/addition answers (casting out nines).

example.question: Digital root of 4789?

notes_list.title: Divisibility by 9
notes_list.basic_overview: A number is divisible by 9 iff its digit sum is divisible by 9.
notes_list.trick: The same digit-sum test works for divisibility by 3.

example.question: Is 7254 divisible by 9?

notes_list.title: Age difference remains constant
notes_list.basic_overview: If no birth/death event is involved, difference between two people's ages remains constant.
notes_list.trick: Use the constant difference to link past, present and future ratios.

example.question: Father is 40 and son is 10. What is the ratio after 5 years?

notes_list.title: Age ratio after t years
notes_list.basic_overview: If present ages are a and b, after t years ratio $$=(a+t):(b+t)$$.
notes_list.trick: Assume present ages are the ratio × x and solve.

example.question: A:B = 4:5 now; after 6 years the ratio is 5:6. Find their ages.

notes_list.title: Past ages
notes_list.trick: Subtract t from each age.

example.question: Father is 3 times son now and 4 times 5 years ago. Find present ages.

notes_list.title: Average age
notes_list.trick: Work with the total sum of ages.

example.question: Average age of 5 persons is 20. A 30-year-old leaves. New average?

notes_list.title: Sum of ages after/before t years
notes_list.basic_overview: Sum of ages of n persons after t years = present sum + n × t (before: − n × t).
notes_list.trick: Every person adds t years.

example.question: Sum of ages of 3 persons is 90. What was it 5 years ago?

notes_list.title: Minute hand speed
notes_list.trick: 360° in 60 minutes.

example.question: Angle moved by the minute hand in 10 minutes?

notes_list.title: Hour hand speed
notes_list.trick: 30° per hour.

example.question: Angle moved by the hour hand in 20 minutes?

notes_list.title: Angle between hands
notes_list.basic_overview: At H:M, angle $$=|30H-5.5M|$$; take the smaller angle if required (if > 180°, subtract from 360°).
notes_list.trick: Use 30H − 5.5M for any time in minutes.

example.question: Angle between the hands at 3:30?

notes_list.title: Coincidence of hands
notes_list.basic_overview: Hands coincide every $$\frac{720}{11}$$ minutes (≈ 65.45 min). In 12 hours: 11 times; in 24 hours: 22 times. Right angle: 22 times in 12 hours (44 in a day); opposite: 11 times in 12 hours.
notes_list.trick: Remember 11-22-44 counts for coincidence, opposite and right angle per day (22, 22, 44).

example.question: How many times do the hands coincide in 12 hours?

notes_list.title: Faulty clocks
notes_list.basic_overview: If a clock gains or loses x minutes per hour, the error after T real hours = x × T minutes.
notes_list.trick: Add the gain to, or subtract the loss from, the real time.

example.question: A clock gains 2 min per hour and is set right at 12 noon. What does it show at 6 PM real time?

notes_list.title: Odd days
notes_list.basic_overview: Seven days make one week; the remainder after dividing total days by 7 gives odd days. 100 years = 5 odd days, 200 = 3, 300 = 1, 400 = 0.
notes_list.trick: Odd days: Sun = 0, Mon = 1, …, Sat = 6.

example.question: Today is Monday. What day will it be after 100 days?

notes_list.title: Leap year
notes_list.basic_overview: A year divisible by 4 is leap, except century years; century years must be divisible by 400.
notes_list.trick: A leap year has 2 odd days; an ordinary year has 1.

example.question: Is 2100 a leap year?
example.solution: No — century year not divisible by 400.

notes_list.title: Days in months
notes_list.basic_overview: 31 days: Jan, Mar, May, Jul, Aug, Oct, Dec; 30 days: Apr, Jun, Sep, Nov; Feb has 28/29.
notes_list.trick: Knuckle method: knuckles = 31 days, valleys = 30 (Feb is the exception).

example.question: Days from 15 Jan to 15 Mar in a non-leap year?

notes_list.title: Day of the week for a date
notes_list.basic_overview: Odd days = (odd days of completed centuries + odd days of completed years + odd days of the months/days of the current year) mod 7.
notes_list.trick: Break the date into centuries, years, then days of the current year.

example.question: Day on 15 Aug 1947?
example.solution: 1600 yrs = 0, 300 yrs = 1, 46 yrs = 46 + 11 leap = 57 → 1; days to 15 Aug = 227 → 3; total = 0 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 5 → Friday.

notes_list.title: Percentage share
notes_list.trick: Use fraction-percentage values (1/8 = 12.5%) for fast mental division.

example.question: Part = 60, total = 400. Share %?

notes_list.title: Ratio from chart values
notes_list.basic_overview: If values are a,b, ratio $$=a:b$$; simplify by HCF.
notes_list.trick: Divide both numbers by their common factors.

example.question: Values are 120 and 180. Ratio?

notes_list.title: Percentage increase in data
notes_list.trick: Always divide by the OLD (base) value.

example.question: Sales rise from 250 to 300. % increase?

notes_list.title: Average from tabular data
notes_list.trick: Use the weighted average when the groups have different sizes.

example.question: Average of 12, 18, 20, 30?

notes_list.title: Percentage point vs percent
notes_list.basic_overview: A change from p₁% to p₂% is (p₂ − p₁) percentage points, but the relative change is $$\frac{p_2-p_1}{p_1}\times100\%$$.
notes_list.trick: Read the question carefully: 'percentage points' → just subtract.

example.question: A rate rises from 20% to 25%. Percentage points and percent change?
Central angle of a sector representing 25%?

notes_list.title: Comparing fractions by cross-multiplication
notes_list.basic_overview: To compare a/b and c/d compare ad and bc.
notes_list.trick: Larger cross-product on the side of the larger fraction.

example.question: Which is greater: 5/7 or 8/11?

sections.title: Quick Tables & Memory Aids (DSSSB Speed Sheet)

notes_list.title: Squares 11–30
notes_list.trick: (n+1)² = n² + 2n + 1 — build each square from the previous one.

example.question: Find √729.

notes_list.title: Cubes 1–15
notes_list.trick: Last digit of a cube identifies the root's last digit (e.g. cube ends in 3 → root ends in 7).

example.question: Find ∛2197.

notes_list.title: Important square roots
notes_list.trick: Use these for surds, trigonometry and mensuration answers.

example.question: Find the diagonal of a square of side 10 cm.

notes_list.title: Multiples of 1/7
notes_list.trick: The same six digits cycle round — only the starting point changes.

example.question: Write 3/7 as a percentage.

notes_list.title: Primes up to 100
notes_list.trick: To test if n is prime, check divisibility by primes up to √n.

example.question: Is 91 prime?

notes_list.title: Unit conversions
notes_list.basic_overview: 1 km = 1000 m; 1 hectare = 10,000 m²; 1 litre = 1000 cm³; 1 quintal = 100 kg; 1 tonne = 1000 kg; 1 inch = 2.54 cm.
notes_list.trick: Convert all quantities to one unit before calculating.

example.question: Convert 2.5 hectares to m².
